## BRK B (Berkshire Hathaway Class B shares): the story as of 8:57 AM CT, Monday Nov 16, 2026

**In one line:** Since October 1, BRK B has been bought as a safe place to hide from the sell-off in AI stocks. It rose about 19% while the S&P 500 fell. It is now at record highs with a key filing due after today's close, and this morning it is falling with the market instead of holding up against it.

### Why it went up
- **Running from AI stocks.** Since October 1, both share classes are up about 19% while the S&P 500 is down 1.2%. In that stretch Class B set 10 record closes and Class A set 11. Last week BRK rose 3.9% against 2.5% for the S&P (CNBC, Nov 14). Fortune ran the headline "haven again as investors flee AI bloodbath" (Nov 7). On a rolling one-month basis the gap over the S&P peaked at 19.2 points on Nov 5 and had narrowed to 16.9 a few days later.
- **The CEO handover has been absorbed.** The stock fell about 15% after Buffett said in May 2025 that he would step down. That loss was fully made back by about Oct 24, and the stock is about 29% above the August 2025 low. 2026 is Greg Abel's first full year as CEO.
- **Spending the cash pile.**
  - Buybacks were $9.6B in Q3, against $4.5B in Q2 and about $14.4B so far this year.
  - Roughly another $2B was bought back in the first four weeks of Q4 (Fortune), so the buying continued as the price rose.
  - Berkshire agreed to buy the homebuilder Taylor Morrison for $6.8B in July.
  - It was a large net buyer of stocks in Q2 ($23.5B bought), including a much bigger Alphabet stake.
- **Analysts.** UBS (Meredith) raised its target from $604 to $628 and rates it Buy. KBW rates it Underperform with a Class A target of $765,000, which is about $510 per B share, well below today's price.

### The weak spots
- **Q3 results (Nov 7).** Operating earnings fell 5.8% to $12.71B. Insurance underwriting fell 43% to $1.35B because GEICO claims were more frequent and more costly, and commissions and advertising rose. Insurance investment income fell 14%. The railroad (BNSF), energy and manufacturing businesses grew. EPS of $5.94 missed the $6.14 estimate. One Yahoo piece says operating earnings rose to $12.98B, which conflicts with CNBC and the other sources, so I'm trusting the $12.71B figure.
- **Valuation.** The stock trades at about 16.5 times trailing earnings (CNBC); Yahoo, on a different basis, puts it at about 12 times earnings and 1.16 times book value. Several columnists say the rally is stretched and that BRK's lead "depends on how long the AI retreat lasts."
- **Smaller items.** Berkshire priced a ¥182B (about $1.1B) yen bond sale at wider spreads than its April sale; a quoted fund manager said sentiment "has become more sensitive." A court approved a $535M talc settlement at National Indemnity, one of its insurers, which closes that matter.

### What's due in the next few sessions (all CT)
- **Today, about 3:05 PM: the Q3 13F filing** (the quarterly list of Berkshire's US stock holdings). It is due today because the deadline rolled over from Saturday, and the last three were filed at about this time on deadline day.
  - The 10-Q already gives the totals: about $2.4B of stocks bought and about $2.8B sold, so a small net seller.
  - Expected: a ninth straight quarter of Bank of America (BAC) selling, estimated at 30 to 40M shares.
  - Possible: more Alphabet, based on a $2.3B rise in cost basis in that category.
  - The filing could show a surprise new stake or an exit. It could move the stock after hours or at Tuesday's open.
- **Today, 11:00 AM:** Fed Chair Warsh gives opening remarks at the Fed's AI and productivity conference. The calendar labels them "Opening Remarks," so a policy signal is unlikely.
- **Tuesday:** US retail sales, and Nvidia's results, its first since Jensen Huang resigned.
- **Wednesday:** Fed minutes and the pricing of Anthropic's IPO.
- **Rates backdrop:** the 10-year Treasury yield is about 5.13%, and markets have largely priced in a December rate hike.

### Reading this morning
- At the open the Nasdaq was down 1.0% to 1.4%, the S&P 500 down about 0.8% to 0.9%, and the Dow down about 0.1%. AI stocks were weak ahead of Nvidia.
- BRK B at -0.6% is beating the S&P only slightly. On a day that should suit a safe-haven trade it is falling with the market.
- That fits buyers getting tired after a stretched run (RSI 81, 3.5 average daily ranges above the 20-day average), better than it fits a fresh flight to safety.

### What would change the picture
**Supports more upside:**
- A bad Nvidia report or a rough Anthropic IPO would renew the flight from AI stocks.
- A 13F with a notable new stake.
- Signs that buybacks are continuing even at these prices.

**Supports a pullback:**
- Strong Nvidia results that bring buyers back to AI stocks. Writers on both sides name this as the main risk.
- A 13F that shows only selling.
- Ordinary mean reversion. The price is about 11% above the 50-day average (531.33), and the 20-day high and record of 596.92 is only about 1.3% above it.

### Caveats
- I found no specific news on BRK this morning. The dip looks like it comes from the overall market.
- Several sources are aggregator or commentary sites. The core figures are confirmed by CNBC and Fortune.
- The "$14.4B" headline I came across turned out to be the year-to-date buyback total, not a single stock purchase.

COIN is falling with crypto, not on news of its own: there is nothing company-specific today. The real story is a slow downgrade of its earnings over the past month, with today's crypto washout on top. One time-sensitive detail is that the CEO's planned share-sale window opens today.

**Price check.** The 7.8% pre-market drop to $117.70 implies Friday closed at about $127.65. That matches your screen's 52-week closing low, so Friday's close was itself the low. Investing.com flagged a new 52-week low at $119.07 this morning, which puts 121.53 about 2% above today's low. The stock opened lower and is bouncing a little; it is not making new lows right now.

**How we got here (last 3 weeks)**
1. **Q3 results, Oct 29 (after the close).**
   - Earnings per share were $2.51 and net income $719M, but almost all of that came from about $715M of gains on Coinbase's own crypto holdings. Underlying adjusted net income was only $78M.
   - Revenue was about $1.2B, flat on Q2, down 35% year on year and slightly below estimates.
   - Trading (transaction) revenue was $590M, down about 44% year on year.
   - Q4 trading revenue was only about $165M through Oct 25, a pace no better than Q3's.
   - The other side of the business held up: subscription and services was $570M, 49% of revenue. Stablecoin income was $307M on a record $22B average USDC (Circle's dollar stablecoin) held in Coinbase products. Prediction markets passed a $200M annual run rate, and derivatives market share rose for a fourth straight quarter.
2. **Binance hack, Oct 29.** About $6.3B was stolen from Binance's hot wallets, reportedly linked to a North Korean hacking group. It hurt confidence across crypto.
3. **Insider sale plans.** The Q3 filing disclosed pre-set trading plans (Rule 10b5-1) covering up to 13.6M shares, about $2.2B at the Oct 29 price. The holders are CEO Brian Armstrong, co-founder Fred Ehrsam and President Emilie Choi.
   - **Armstrong's plan, up to 8.17M shares, runs from today, Nov 16, through October 2027.** It has preset price thresholds that I couldn't find.
   - The filing lists possible sales, not completed ones. Still, a supply overhang that becomes active today is real for a 1–10 session view.
4. **Oct 30 close: down 10.6% to $143.54.**
   - A wave of price-target cuts followed the results.
   - On Nov 2, Morgan Stanley (Cyprys) downgraded to Underweight and cut its target from $258 to $120. It cut its 2027 revenue forecast by 28% and its 2027 EBITDA forecast by 47%, saying "confidence in the earnings recovery has deteriorated."
   - Barclays also has $120. KBW cut to $221 but kept Outperform. The consensus target is about $199–226, depending on the provider.
5. **Nov 6:** a new 52-week low of about $131.55 intraday, close about $134.76. A partial bounce followed, to about $137 on Nov 11, before Friday's close at about $127.65.

**Today's driver: a crypto crash on top of a hawkish Fed**
- Bitcoin fell below $62,000 on Saturday, a four-month low, with about $2B of leveraged positions liquidated (about $1.68B of it bets on prices rising).
  - It posted a sixth straight weekly loss, closing the week at about $65,351, and fell below its 200-week average.
  - It is down about 17% in November and was about $64,600–65,500 at 8:39 AM CT.
  - Ether briefly hit about $1,800 around 7:38 AM CT.
- The Crypto Fear & Greed Index sits at 10, extreme fear.
- US spot bitcoin ETFs (exchange-traded funds holding bitcoin directly) had about $1.1B of outflows last week; another source says nearly $3B.

- Macro:
  - October CPI came in hot (core +0.3%), and futures price a December rate hike at about 85–99%. The Fed meets Dec 8–9.
  - The 10-year Treasury yield is above 5.1% and the dollar index (DXY) above 103.
  - The Nasdaq was down about 1.15% at 8:39 AM CT.
  - This week brings the Fed minutes and Nvidia earnings.
- Pre-market, COIN was down 6.4–7.8%, MSTR about 8%, Circle about 8%, Robinhood about 5–6%. COIN at −4.8% is now doing better than its peers.

**Reading the story for 1–10 sessions**
- **Bear case.** Trading revenue, the main earnings engine, is shrinking and has not bottomed. A crypto bear market cuts volumes further, so Q4 trading revenue likely tracks bitcoin down. The Fed is turning hawkish just as risk appetite breaks. Insider selling may begin today. Underweight targets ($120) are now at the stock price, so the bears have been proven right and there is no obvious value anchor. Every trend measure on your screen points down.
- **Bull/bounce case.**
  - Positioning is washed out: liquidations, a sentiment reading of 10, RSI 30, 2.8 average daily ranges below the 20-day average, heavy volume, and the stock bouncing off $119 rather than breaking it.
  - Higher rates actually help Coinbase's stablecoin interest income (about $307M a quarter), and record USDC balances cushion the shrinking trading business.
  - Any bitcoin relief rally would lift COIN by more than bitcoin, since COIN moves more than bitcoin does.
  - Earnings are about 60 sessions away, so there is no event risk from results.

agents.report:
The story is simple: BMNR (BitMine Immersion Technologies) is effectively a leveraged-feeling wrapper on Ether. It holds about 6.08M ETH, worth roughly 94% of its assets, and its stock price follows ETH's price. Over the next 1 to 10 sessions, the trade is a bet on whether Ether gets past this week's selling. Small, partly offsetting factors are the shares trading a little below their assets, a buyback, and its biggest buyer stepping back.

**What the company is**
- It used to mine Bitcoin. Since June 30, 2025 it has been the largest corporate holder of Ether, a Strategy-style treasury company. Its chairman, Tom Lee (Fundstrat), is also its main promoter. It raised about $13.2B in fiscal 2026 by selling 395M new shares.
- **Holdings (company release, as of Saturday Nov 15):**
  - 6,077,745 ETH at $1,823 each, which is 4.97% of all ETH in existence.
  - $448M in cash and securities and 216 BTC.
  - About $247M in other investments: $180M in Beast Industries and $67M in Eightco.
  - Total of about $11.8B.
  - It added only 7,653 ETH last week, against 9,587, 10,452 and 12–15k in earlier weeks.
- **Staking:** It stakes (locks up to earn network rewards) about 5.23M ETH, 86% of its holdings, mostly through its own validator business, MAVAN (Made in America Validator Network). At current prices that runs about $245–285M a year. That income is in ETH, so it shrinks when ETH falls.
- **Preferred stock:** 3.5M shares of 9.5% perpetual preferred (BMNP), with about $350M owed to holders ahead of common shareholders and roughly $33M a year in dividends. There is no meaningful debt.
- **Fiscal year to August 31 (10-K out about Nov 12–13):**
  - Net loss of $6.31B, almost all of it paper losses on ETH. The ETH cost $19.9B and was worth $14.6B at year end.
  - Revenue of $124.8M, ahead of the $119.8M analysts expected.
  - One article says the filing reports ineffective financial-reporting controls. Another says it found nothing on controls. I couldn't confirm it.

**Valuation (my estimate)**
- I'm using about 625M shares. The count is not disclosed; this figure comes from the Nov 13 market cap of about $11.56B at $18.45, and a tracker estimate of about 624.8M.
- At ETH near $1,807:
  - ETH is worth about $10.98B, plus about $0.71B of everything else, minus $0.35B of preferred.
  - That leaves about $11.34B, or roughly $18.1 per share.
- At $16.73 the stock trades at about 0.92 times its assets, an 8% discount.
- Each $100 move in ETH is worth about $0.97 per share.
- Management buys back stock when it trades below asset value:
  - It has bought 22.9M shares this year at an average of $17.48 ($399.6M), including 2.04M at $22.48 in the week to Oct 25.
  - The Nov 9 and Nov 16 releases mention no buybacks. That's worth noting, because the discount is wider now.
  - Sources disagree on what is left in the program. Some say $3.6B of $4B remains; Lee said on Oct 7 that the earlier $4B program was finished Aug 17.

**How the narrative has turned**
1. **ETH is collapsing.**
   - ETH fell from $2,356 (Oct 25) to $2,234 (Nov 8) to $1,823 (Nov 15).
   - Over the weekend it hit about $1,711, then bounced to roughly $1,800–1,830 this morning.
   - It is down about 18% on the week, about 26% on the month and about 42% on the year.
   - Daily RSI is about 25 and it sits far below its 50/100/200-day averages (about $2,260–2,283).
   - US spot Ether ETFs have had seven straight weeks of outflows, $399M last week; one more would tie the record. Bitcoin hit about $62k, liquidations topped about $2B, and the Fear & Greed index reads 10.
2. **Lee blames liquidity, not fundamentals.** His Nov 14–16 explanation:
   - The AI and Nvidia stock sell-off forced margin selling, especially among Asian retail traders.
   - People are raising cash for the Anthropic IPO, priced around Nov 18 with Nasdaq trading about Nov 19. Robinhood retail allocations are part of this.
   - Funds from the late-October Binance hack (about $6.3B, attributed to North Korea) are moving.
   - His analogy: ETH fell 39% in the eight weeks before SpaceX's June 2026 IPO and bottomed three trading days before it priced.
   - That puts his implied bottom around now, which is the bull case for a 1–10 session bounce.
   - It is the chairman talking his own book, and the analogy rests on a single past case.
3. **Its biggest buyer is stepping back.** Lee has said 5% of supply is a "hard cap," and BitMine is about 43k ETH away. Weekly buying is already shrinking.
   - For BMNR shareholders this is mixed. There is no more dilution from stock sales, and money shifts to buybacks.
   - For ETH, one of its steadiest buyers is about to leave. The stock rallied on Nov 11 when this was announced, then gave it all back.
4. **Price path.** $18.45 on Nov 13 (−5.6%), about $17.52 on Nov 14 (−5%), $16.73 now. The 52-week range is $12.80 to $42.09.
   - B. Riley kept its Buy rating but cut its target from $34 to $27. Only two analysts cover it, and their $48.80 average target means little.

**What matters for the trade**
- **Today's drop:** BMNR is down 4.9% even though ETH this morning (about $1,800–1,830) is close to or above its weekend level. I could not find Friday's 3:00 PM CT ETH price, so I can't tell whether this is BMNR catching up to the weekend drop or the discount widening. If ETH is flat to up since Friday's close, BMNR is lagging its own assets, a sign that holders of the wrapper are giving up.
- **Within the next 3–4 sessions:** The Anthropic pricing (about Nov 18) and debut (about Nov 19) is a dated catalyst. Lee's thesis predicts the cash drain ends then. If ETH does not recover after the debut, that explanation is gone.
- **Signals to watch:** The ETH level ($1,711 weekend low, then about $1,750); Ether ETF flows (an eighth week of outflows would tie the record); and the Nov 23 weekly release, which will show whether buybacks resumed and whether the 5% cap has been reached.
- **Risks:** A falling ETH price squeezes staking income and the preferred dividend's cash cover, though only slowly. Shares outstanding are not known exactly. Earnings are about 39 sessions away and outside the window.

All holdings and staking figures are BitMine's own unaudited weekly releases. Lee's market views are opinion from an interested party.

IBIT (BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust, which simply holds bitcoin) is down today because of a weekend bitcoin crash it couldn't trade through. Most of today's 5.2% drop is not new selling. Bitcoin trades all weekend and IBIT does not, so this morning's gap mostly catches IBIT up to Saturday's crash. The deeper story is a slide that has lasted six weeks, driven mainly by interest rates.

## Today's move is mostly catch-up
- One IBIT share holds about 0.000569 bitcoin, so 36.90 implies bitcoin near $64,900. Friday's IBIT close of about 38.9 implies bitcoin near $68,400, which matches reports of about $68,000 late Friday.
- Bitcoin fell below $62,000 on Saturday (about $62,000–62,100), its lowest since July. About $2 billion of leveraged bets on higher prices were force-closed.
- It bounced to about $65,500 around 8:39 AM CT today, then slipped back to $64,100–64,400. CoinDesk called the bounce "a dead-cat bounce until proven otherwise."
- The heavy volume is the backlog of weekend selling clearing at once, not news from this morning.

**Price map** (bitcoin price → IBIT, my arithmetic):

| Bitcoin | IBIT | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| $57,700 | 32.84 | IBIT's 52-week low; bitcoin's July 1 low was $57,737, so they match |
| $60,000 | 34.1 | Round-number support analysts are watching |
| $62,000 | 35.3 | Weekend low; a daily close below it opens $60,000 |
| $67,000 | 38.1 | Resistance analysts say must be retaken |
| $67,700 | 38.49 | IBIT's 20-day low, now above the price |
| $70,000 | 39.8 | Next resistance |

## How it got here
1. **The 2025 peak and a long decline.** Bitcoin peaked at about $126,000 on October 6, 2025, then fell for most of 2026. It hit about $58,000 on June 25 and $57,737 on July 1.
2. **A summer recovery.** It rallied to about $87,000 in early October on a weak jobs report and hopes the Fed would stop raising rates.
3. **The new slide.** It fell to about $75,000 in early November and about $62,000 on Saturday. That is down roughly 17% in November and six straight weekly losses.

## What is driving it
1. **Rates.** This is the main driver. October consumer inflation was hot (+0.4% for the month), and October producer prices were up 6.5% from a year ago. The CME FedWatch tool puts the odds of a December 9 Fed hike at about 99%, and some now talk of a 50-basis-point hike. The 10-year Treasury yield is about 5.15%, and the dollar index is above 103. One headline put it this way: bitcoin "trades like a rates bet, not an inflation hedge."
2. **ETF outflows.** IBIT has seen money leave for 11 straight sessions through Friday, November 13. It lost about $2.12 billion in November, roughly 90% of all money leaving US spot bitcoin ETFs this month. Friday alone was −$143.5 million.
   - The average spot-ETF holder's cost was estimated at about $73,000 in June and $82,000 after the fall rally. At $64,000 that holder is likely underwater. These figures come from older estimates; I found no current one.
   - Today's flow numbers come out after the close tonight.
3. **The Binance hack.** About $6.3 billion was stolen from Binance (the largest crypto exchange) on October 30, the largest crypto theft on record, blamed on North Korea. Binance says it will cover the losses, and roughly $2.4–3 billion has reportedly been frozen. It hurt confidence just as the outflows began.
4. **Tech and AI stocks.** AI stocks have been selling off, and the Nasdaq (the tech-heavy US index) was down about 1.15% early today. Crypto-linked stocks are down 5–10% before the open, including Strategy (MSTR) at about −8%.
5. **Corporate buyers have run dry.** Strategy is the largest corporate bitcoin holder, at 850,849 BTC bought at an average of $75,452.
   - Since June its shares have traded below the value of the bitcoin it holds. It has sold 6,948 BTC in 2026, and its board approved bitcoin sales of up to $1.25 billion to fund a cash reserve, dividends and buybacks.
   - Last week it bought only 485 BTC. CoinDesk suggested Strategy and Strive "might be the only buyers left."
6. **Geopolitics and oil.** The US–Iran conflict continues: Iran's Revolutionary Guard reportedly attacked a US base in Bahrain, and a third US aircraft carrier is expected in the region today. Higher oil prices feed inflation, which feeds rate fears. I could not confirm the November details beyond one market report.

## Sentiment and positioning
- The crypto Fear & Greed index is at 10 (extreme fear), down from 20.
- Bitcoin's own 14-day RSI is about 23, close to IBIT's 24.
- About 73% of coins held by recent buyers are at a loss. Stablecoin supply (cash parked inside crypto) fell about $17 billion in a month.
- Holders of more than 1,000 BTC bought about 47,000 BTC during the fall, but overall 30-day demand is about −284,000 BTC.
- I found no current data on funding rates or options positioning.

## This week's catalysts (all Central time)
- **Mon 11/16:** IBIT flow data after the close.
- **Tue 11/17:** October retail sales, 7:30 AM CT.
- **Wed 11/18:** Nvidia earnings after the close. This matters because of the AI-stock link.
- **Thu 11/19:** Fed meeting minutes at 1:00 PM CT, jobless claims, and Anthropic's planned Nasdaq debut. A large new tech listing could pull money from other speculative holdings.
- **Ongoing:** Iran headlines, and any sign of Strategy selling bitcoin.

## The two sides for a 1–10 session hold
- **For a rebound:** IBIT is deeply oversold, sentiment is at extreme fear, leverage was flushed out over the weekend, and large holders are buying. Bitcoin is already bouncing off $62,000, and the June–July lows near $58,000 drew buyers before.
- **Against:** The cause is not fading. The Fed is set to hike, yields are above 5%, and money has left IBIT for 11 straight sessions. ETF holders are underwater and could keep selling, and Strategy has gone from steady buyer to possible seller.

  - IBIT inflows would be the clearest sign of a turn.

- One forecaster expected bitcoin to chop between $62,000 and $66,100 this week, and another expected a final bottom of $42,000–44,000 in October–December 2026. Treat both as opinions.

agents.report:
XLP (the Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR, a fund of the S&P 500's grocery, household-goods, beverage, tobacco and big-box retail stocks) is near the end of a two-month move out of AI and tech into defensive stocks. The move is real and well reported, but it is late and stretched. This week brings Nvidia, Target and Walmart earnings, and any of them could stop it or speed it up. Today's open matters more than the screen suggests: XLP spiked to a new high and has been sliding back since.

## The story behind the move

**It is a flight from tech.** The rally is mostly about where investors are pulling money from, not about staples companies doing better.
- In October, MSCI's global staples index rose 10.6%, its best month since 1998, while global tech fell more than 13%.
- Since the Nasdaq 100 peaked on October 6, Walmart is up about 15% and Procter & Gamble and Coca-Cola about 10% each.
- The causes cited are doubts that AI data-centre spending will pay off, hedge funds cutting tech, and Citi downgrading tech to neutral while expecting defensives to keep leading into 2027.
- On November 13, XLP led all sectors at +1.3% while XLK (the tech sector fund) fell 2.7% and SMH (a chip-stock fund) fell 4.1%.

**The midterms added to it.** On November 4, the day after Democrats won both chambers, XLP set an all-time high at about 8:56 AM CT and finished up 3.4% that day. Money went into economy-linked stocks outside tech; Walmart rose 3%.

**The economy pushes the same way.**
- The Fed raised rates in September and held at 3.75–4.00% in October, with two members wanting another hike. A December hike is being discussed after hot inflation data.
- The 10-year Treasury yield is about 5.13%.
- Brent crude is around $94–96 because of the Iran war. That makes staples look safer than discretionary stocks (companies selling things people can put off buying).
- Year to date, staples are up about 17%, discretionary about 4% and the S&P 500 about 10%, per Chase on November 10.

**Strength is broad, not just a few names.** A November 8 rotation report ranked XLP first of 11 sectors, with every measured holding above its 20-week trend. Its model rated XLP "strong / durable leadership" and overweight.

## The case against chasing it

**It is stretched and expensive.**
- Lance Roberts' November 16 note puts staples 9.2% above their 50-day relative trend, one of the two most stretched sectors with health care, and advises trimming extended defensives into strength.
- HSBC calls the rotation into defensives "extreme" and "overdone." It notes Walmart, XLP's largest holding, trades at about 40 times forward earnings, near a record, while Nvidia is at about 13 times.
- XLP's own P/E is about 25.6 (21.5 forward), and its dividend yield of about 2.4% has to compete with a 5%+ 10-year Treasury.

**The last test of this level failed.** On November 5, XLP hit 93.40 intraday on 37 million shares, its heaviest day in the period, and closed at 91.25. It fell to 90.08 the next day. That 93.40 is the 20-day high your screen lists. Since then XLP has ground back up to a record close of 92.35 last Friday.

**Today it went above that high and is falling back.** At 8:50 AM CT, stockanalysis showed:
- Day's range 92.87–93.48, so the high came early and was a new intraday peak just above 93.40.
- Price 92.87–92.91, at or near the day's low.
- 3.7 million shares traded.

The screen's 92.78 at 8:55 AM CT is below that low. XLP is still up 0.5% and above Friday's record close, but so far the open looks like a failed second push through 93.40, not a clean breakout.

## What's coming in the next one to ten sessions

All times CT:
- **Today:** Fed Chair Warsh speaks at 11:00 AM. Tyson (TSN, a small XLP holding) is up about 10% on earnings, a staples-specific tailwind.
- **Tuesday, November 17:** October retail sales at 7:30 AM. Nvidia reports after the close, its first report since Jensen Huang resigned as CEO; Nvidia is down about 13% in five days. A strong report could start money moving back into tech and out of defensives. A weak one would likely extend the staples trade.
- **Wednesday, November 18:** Target (TGT, about 4% of XLP) reports, expected before the open but not confirmed. Fed minutes at 1:00 PM.
- **Thursday, November 19:** Walmart (WMT, 11.2% of XLP) reports before the open. It guided to 3–3.75% sales growth and EPS of $0.62–0.64, and at 40 times earnings the bar is high. Anthropic's IPO, targeting about $1.4 trillion, is also expected to begin trading Thursday and is framed as a test of appetite for AI stocks.
- **Friday, November 20:** final University of Michigan sentiment and inflation expectations, which carry extra weight while a hike is on the table.
- **No dividend in the window.** XLP's next ex-dividend date is expected in late December.

## Fund facts

Holdings as of November 16, 2026, per stockanalysis:
- **Top holdings:** Walmart 11.2%, Costco 9.7%, P&G 7.8%, Coca-Cola 7.6%, Philip Morris 6.1%, Altria 4.6%, Colgate 4.5%, Mondelez 4.3%, PepsiCo 4.2%, Target 4.1%. The top 10 make up 64%.
- **Size and cost:** $14.9 billion in assets, 0.08% expense ratio.
- **Recent range:** 52-week range 76.23–93.48. XLP has risen from 81.70 on October 7 to 92.35, about 13% in under six weeks.

## How it fits together

The theme is real, broad, and driven by events still under way: AI doubts, Fed hikes, high oil and post-election rotation. The setup this morning is weaker than the screen's breakout reading suggests:
- the price is a second attempt at the 93.40 level that reversed sharply on November 5;
- today's push above it has already faded from 93.48;
- strategists are explicitly calling defensives stretched;
- the stock carrying 11% of the fund (Walmart) reports Thursday at a near-record multiple;
- Nvidia's report Tuesday night could reverse the rotation.

The trend gives some backing for holding over several days. The near-term path depends on Nvidia and Walmart, and a fade back below about 92.35 today would repeat the November 5 pattern.

## SLV (iShares Silver Trust, an ETF that holds physical silver bars) — research brief, 8:57 AM CT, Mon 2026-11-16

Note: I hit the web-search limit for this turn before I could check what Fed official Williams said this morning (8:05 AM CT). That gap is flagged below. A follow-up message can pick it up.

### Today
- Spot silver is about $47.26–47.34, down 2.4–3% and at a one-year low. Each SLV share holds roughly 0.905 oz, which puts fair value near $42.8, so your 42.74 matches spot. There is no gap between the ETF price and the metal.
- **Today's selling looks like risk-off, not more rate fears.** The dollar index (about 103.4) and Treasury yields (10-year about 5.14%, 2-year about 4.85%) were roughly flat overnight. What fell was AI and chip stocks: Taiwan's market down about 6%, Korea's about 4%, the Nikkei 2.4%, and Nasdaq futures about 1.3% before the open. Silver fell more than three times as much as gold (gold down about 0.6–0.7%). ActionForex describes silver trading like a high-beta risk asset rather than a safe haven.
- The gold-to-silver price ratio is about 81–82, above its prior high of 80.1. Silver keeps losing ground to gold.
- Behind this is Nvidia's leadership turmoil: Huang was ousted, and there are reports of an outside-CEO push and of Huang talking about a return. Nvidia fell 12.75% last week, its worst week since April 2025.

### How it got here (the story)
1. **Speculative peak.** Silver roughly doubled in 2025, then rose more than 50% in January 2026 to a record of about $121.6–121.7 on Jan 29. It then lost about 30% in one day after CME raised margins and leveraged positions were forced out. The BIS (Bank for International Settlements) blamed leveraged ETPs (exchange-traded products) and systematic selling for making it worse.
2. **Slow bleed since.** Price is down about 61% from the peak and about 31% since the 2025 close. The drivers:
   - **Rising rates.** The Fed is in a hiking cycle; the target range is now 3.75–4.00%. October CPI was hot (core up 0.3% for a third straight month).
   - **Dollar and yields.** The 10-year yield is above 5% and the dollar is at 2026 highs. Silver pays no interest, so it suffers in this setting.
   - **India stopped buying.** Import restrictions came in May–June, and net Indian absorption fell from about 100 Moz (million ounces) in 2025 to about 10 Moz.
   - **Solar uses less silver.** Solar demand is forecast to drop from 186.6 Moz to about 151 Moz as each panel uses less, and BloombergNEF expects 2026 solar installations to fall about 10.8%.
3. **Breakdown in the last two weeks.** Silver was about $52.5 on Nov 9 and about $48.5 at Friday's close, down about 10% in a week and about 17% in a month. The trigger was hot CPI on Nov 10 and PPI on Nov 13. Markets now price about a 91–94% chance of a 0.25-point Fed hike on Dec 9 and an 8–13% chance of a 0.5-point hike. Governor Waller said he would back a 0.5-point hike if inflation keeps accelerating. Friday's high of about $50.9 was sold to $48.4.

### Is the "deficit" story intact?
- **Weaker than it was.** The Silver Institute / Metals Focus interim review (Nov 12) cut the 2026 deficit to 35 Moz from 46.3 Moz. That would still be a sixth straight deficit. But funds are expected to release about 45 Moz, so including fund flows the market is in a roughly 10 Moz surplus. Metals Focus has pointed to a theoretical surplus of about 37 Moz in 2027.
- Its stated view is that the price case now depends on funds buying physical silver, not on a shortage.
- Coin and bar demand is down to about 215 Moz, and US retail buying is at its lowest since 2010. London vaults held about 932 Moz at the end of September, close to a four-year high.

### Flows and positioning (could cut either way)
- **ETF holdings are not collapsing.** Global silver ETF holdings were about flat to slightly up on Friday (814.4 to 814.5 Moz, per SP Angel). Funds have bought back about 24 Moz since late June. SLV still holds about 24.4 Moz less than at the end of 2025, but SEC filings show net creations in Q3. So far this looks like a futures and macro selloff, not ETF holders running.
- **Speculators are barely long.** Managed money on COMEX was about +4,000 contracts net long (Nov 3), versus about +38,800 roughly a year ago. That is near a washout level, so there is little long positioning left to be forced out, and any short covering could drive a bounce. This comes from third-party sites and I did not check it against the CFTC.
- **Very oversold short-term.** The 4-hour RSI is about 21 and your daily RSI reads 29.

### Levels people are watching (spot, and the SLV equivalent at about ×0.905)

| Next support (ActionForex 38.2% projection) | 46.48 | ~42.1 |

SLV is already trading at about the equivalent of the $46.48 support.

### Catalysts over the next 1–10 sessions (Central time)
- **Today:** Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks at 11:00 AM CT; he is not expected to give rate guidance. Hammack, who dissented in October in favor of a hike, speaks at 1:15 PM CT. Williams spoke at 8:05 AM CT; I could not check what he said.
- **Tue Nov 17:** Retail sales and industrial production at 7:30 AM CT. **Nvidia earnings after the close.** Options price about a 7.8% move, and this is the main risk-sentiment event for silver.
- **Wed Nov 18:** FOMC minutes at 1:00 PM CT. Anthropic's IPO is reportedly pricing.
- **Wed–Thu:** APEC meetings in Shenzhen, including a reported Trump–Xi–Putin meeting.
- **Thu Nov 19:** Jobless claims at 7:30 AM CT. **Fri Nov 20:** University of Michigan sentiment.
- **Dec 9:** FOMC decision. A 0.25-point hike is about fully priced, so only a 0.5-point hike would be a fresh shock.

### Bull case vs bear case
- **Bounce:** Silver is very oversold and on 2.4× normal volume, which looks like a capitulation day. Speculators hold almost no longs. ETF holders are not redeeming. Today's drop is risk-off spillover rather than new rate news. A calm Nvidia print or a Warsh speech without new guidance could set off a sharp bounce back toward about 45 on SLV.
- **Further decline:** Every trend is down: below the 50- and 200-day averages, a death cross, and the gold/silver ratio breaking out. Rates are still rising with more hikes priced into 2027, and the dollar is at 2026 highs. The deficit story has turned into a surplus once fund flows are counted, and Indian buying has collapsed. If Nvidia disappoints, risk-off feeds silver's high-beta selling. The projected downside target is about 38 on SLV. Commentary notes there is "no clear sign of bottoming."

## 1. Nvidia without Huang
- **What happened:** Huang resigned on November 12 after reports of affairs, one with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO.

## What Strategy is now
Strategy is effectively a leveraged bitcoin holding company. Its old software business no longer matters to the price.

## What happened this week
1. **Index removal.** On November 11, MSCI confirmed it will drop Strategy from the MSCI USA Index and its other global indexes after the close on Monday, November 30. Its new rule treats Strategy as a "non-operating" company, one whose value comes from the assets it holds rather than a business it runs. Funds tracking MSCI hold about 13 million shares, about 3.1% of the share count and worth roughly $1.4B at today's price. Strategy says that is less than one day's normal trading volume. Saylor called the decision "discriminatory." A widely quoted $8.8B selling figure is an older JPMorgan estimate that assumed other index providers would follow; none has.    - only $33.4M on 485 BTC, at $68,887 each

What looks like the bull case is that the beef losses have bottomed and the company is generating more cash. I also ran out of web searches before I could read the earnings call, so call commentary is missing.

## What happened today
Tyson reported fiscal Q4 2026 before the open (from the company's 8-K):
- **Quarter:** adjusted EPS was $0.61, down 47% from $1.15. Estimates differ by source ($0.53, $0.60 or $0.65), so it was a beat or a miss depending on the source. Sales were $14.59B, up 5.2%, but only because of an extra week; excluding that week and legal accruals, sales fell 4%. Adjusted operating income was $361M, down 41%. GAAP EPS was a loss of $0.22, driven by $254M of restructuring charges and $124M of legal accruals.
- **Segments, Q4 adjusted operating income:**

| Segment | Q4 2026 | Q4 2025 |
|---|---|---|
| Beef | -$171M | -$52M |
| Chicken | $389M | $562M |
| Pork | $16M | $47M |
| Prepared Foods | $321M | $278M |
| International | $49M | $40M |

- **Full year 2026:** adjusted EPS was $3.44, down 17%. Free cash flow was $1.66B, up $486M. Debt fell $1.08B and the company bought back $427M of stock.
- **Fiscal 2027 guidance:**
  - Total adjusted operating income: $1.7B to $2.15B (midpoint about $1.93B, against $1.98B in 2026).
  - Beef: a loss of $300M to a profit of $100M, against a $654M loss in 2026.
  - Chicken: $1.3B to $1.6B, down from $1.86B, partly on higher feed costs.
  - Prepared Foods: $1.25B to $1.4B, about flat.
  - Sales: down 3.5% to 5.5%, against a consensus of about -1% (LSEG).
  - Free cash flow: $0.8B to $1.3B. Capex: $1.1B to $1.4B, up from $0.77B.
- **Dividend:** raised 2%, to $0.52 a quarter.

**My EPS estimate (my arithmetic, not company guidance):** take the midpoint operating income, subtract about $360M of interest, apply a 25% tax rate and use about 355M shares. That gives roughly $3.30 for 2027, in a range of about $2.90 to $3.80, so EPS would be flat to slightly down. One aggregator shows a 2027 consensus of $4.59, which is probably out of date. If it were current, the guidance would be a big miss, which doesn't fit a 10% rally. I could not get a reliable current consensus.

## The bull case for the rally
None of the coverage gives a cause, so this is my reading of the guidance:
- **Beef has hit bottom:** guidance points to beef going from -$654M to about -$100M at the midpoint, an improvement of about $550M. That improvement largely offsets lower chicken profit.
- **Beef is being restructured:** in August Tyson said it would close or sell the Joslin (Illinois), Eagle Mountain (Utah) and Pasco (Washington) beef sites. Production moves to Dakota City, Holcomb and Amarillo, with a new cattle supply deal (Allied Beef) and a second shift added at Amarillo.
- **Cattle supply may improve:** USDA began reopening Mexican cattle imports from August 24, after the screwworm ban. TSN rose about 7% when that was announced in July, and analysts expected the benefit to show up in 2027.
- **Cash and balance sheet:** free cash flow is strong, debt is falling, the dividend went up, and the yield is about 3.2% at $65.
- **New CEO:** Jeff Schomburger replaced Donnie King in early October. A guide that looks "kitchen-sinked" (set low on purpose) is a common first move for a new CEO.
- **Precedent:** in August the stock dipped and then closed up 2.5% on a deeper beef-loss forecast, as chicken strength outweighed beef. This looks like the same pattern.

## The bear case
- **Chicken is past its peak:** guidance implies a 14% to 30% decline, the segment that has been carrying the company.
- **Sales:** the guided decline is much steeper than consensus.
- **Cash:** free cash flow falls and capex rises.
- **Beef uncertainty:** the $400M-wide beef range shows management can't see the cattle cycle clearly. The herd is near a 70-75 year low.
- **Legal costs keep coming:** $393M of legal accruals this year.
- **Quality of earnings:** adjusted operating income fell 41% in the quarter.

## Timing and price action
- **Premarket to open:** early stories had the stock up only about 1.2% in premarket. The earnings call was at 9:00 AM ET (8:00 AM CT), before the 8:30 AM CT open. So the jump to +10.5% most likely came during or after the call, from something said there, short covering, or both. I could not confirm which.
- **Volume:** a live snapshot at 8:51 AM CT showed $65.10 on about 1.2M shares, against a normal 3–4M a day.
- **Run-up into the report:** the stock was already up from $51.70 (October 7) to $58.82 (November 13 close), about 14% in five weeks. That included an unexplained 5.4% jump on November 4 on 5.6M shares, and heavy volume of 7.2M on November 13, the day before the report. Today adds about 10.5%, so the stock is up about 26% in six weeks.
- **Analysts before the report:** of 13 analysts, 5 rate it Buy, 7 Hold and 1 Sell. Consensus price targets range from about $65.6 to $70.7, depending on the source. Piper Sandler is Overweight; one report has its target raised to $75, another has it cut from $66 to $56 on October 7. JPMorgan upgraded to Overweight with a $63 target on September 18. At $65 the stock already sits around the average target.
- **Resistance:** the 52-week high is $68.26, about 5% above the current price. One older quote showed a range high of $69.48.

## For the 1-10 session decision
- **For a trade:** a real fundamental catalyst, a turn in the beef profit trajectory with a defined path, volume about 2.9 times normal, a new CEO resetting expectations, and a stock that was already trending up.
- **Against a trade:** the headline guidance is weak, the stock is extended (RSI 79, 3.8 average ranges above its 20-day average), it is near consensus targets with $68 resistance close by, and the cause of the rally is unconfirmed.
- **What decides it:** whether analysts raise targets or upgrade today and tomorrow. Price targets above $70 would support follow-through. Holding above about $62–63, roughly the old range top near $60 plus half of today's gap, would show buyers defending the gap.

**1. The low point (late September).** FCN closed at 130.45 on Sep 24, 2026. The stock had been out of favour for over a year. In February it was 160.91, down 16% over twelve months. - **Revenue:** a record $1.013B, up 5.9%, with all five segments growing.
- **Adjusted EPS:** $3.84 against a $2.74 consensus, up 48% year on year. GAAP EPS was $2.35 after a $46M charge for layoffs.
- **Profit margin:** adjusted EBITDA (operating profit before interest, tax and depreciation) was 15.2% of revenue, up from 13.7%.
- **Guidance:** full-year adjusted EPS raised to $9.50–$10.00 from $9.10–$9.70. Revenue guidance kept at $3.94–$4.10B.
- **Cost cuts:** about 4% of staff, mostly in the Middle East and UK, for about $80M a year in savings. Management called these exits from investments that weren't working, not a response to a downturn.

## Dynatrace (DT): what's behind the drop

**Bottom line:** DT is not falling right now. It is sitting still after a 35% collapse from its high. Since the Nov 6 close it has traded in a tight $42.69–45.53 band. Daily lows have been creeping up (42.69, then 43.37, then 43.84), and volume has fallen from 22.6M shares on earnings day to about 5M. The 200-day average ($44.81) sits right above the price and has capped it. The dispute is over one thing: whether a missed growth number was just a few big deals closing late or the start of a real slowdown. No scheduled event in the next 1–10 sessions will settle it. Q4 is where most of the year's renewals land, so the answer comes with the February report.

### How it got here
1. **The rally (spring to Oct 13).** The stock went from a 52-week low of about $32 to an intraday high of $66.30 on Oct 13. Investors bought it as a way to profit from companies putting AI agents into production. Dynatrace sells "observability" software, which watches whether a company's apps and systems are working. Other boosts:
   - It bought Arize, a startup that monitors AI models, for $915M (announced in August).
   - It won FedRAMP High status, a security clearance that opens up US government work.
   - UBS raised its price target to $74 and Needham upgraded the stock to Buy.
   - At the top it was valued at more than 100 times earnings.
2. **The slide into earnings (Oct 13 to Nov 2): about 15% down, from $65 to $55.13.** This was mostly a broad selloff in software stocks plus investors trimming before the report. It fell 5% on Oct 30 and 4.4% on Nov 2.
3. **Earnings on Nov 3 (fiscal Q2 2027): down 14.7% to $47.03 on 22.6M shares.** The quarter itself beat: revenue $580M (+17%) against $568M expected, and adjusted EPS $0.54 against $0.49. What hurt:
   - **New annual subscription revenue was weak.** Net new ARR (the yearly subscription revenue added in the quarter) was $70M, flat with a year ago. A handful of large existing customers delayed planned expansions, leaving it a "high single-digit millions" short. Management says those deals were not lost and several closed early in Q3.
   - **Customers expanded less.** Net retention, which measures how much more existing customers spend, slipped 1 point to 109%.
   - **Profit and cash guidance went down.** Full-year EPS guidance fell to $1.88–1.90 from $1.97–1.99, below the $1.98 analysts expected. Two causes: Arize lowers the operating margin by about 1.75 points, and about 14M extra shares are counted from the $1.4B convertible bond issued in August. Free cash flow guidance was trimmed to $600–605M.
   - **Growth guidance without Arize stayed the same.** Subscription growth excluding Arize is still guided at 15.5–16.5%; management chose not to raise it.
   - **The CFO will retire by the end of the fiscal year.**
   - **Q3 EPS guidance of $0.44–0.45 was below the $0.48 consensus.**
4. **Further drop on Nov 5: down 6.6% to $43.70.** This was most likely spillover from Datadog (DDOG), its biggest competitor, which reported Nov 4 and fell about 13–19%. Datadog's sales growth was strong (+35%), but its Q4 forecast assumes its largest customer, an AI company, cuts spending to its contract minimum. That makes investors worry that AI-driven monitoring spending is concentrated and could be cut. On DT's call, its CEO said he had seen no evidence that customers' scrutiny of AI spending delayed any Dynatrace deal. The timing points to a sector-wide reaction, but I couldn't confirm the exact cause of the Nov 5 move.
5. **Since then (Nov 6 to today):** the stock has held the $42.69–45.53 band. Trefis counted a 9-day losing streak of about 32%, worth about $6B in market value, and said the drop was mostly Dynatrace's own story, not the market's. Today it opened at $44.30, has traded between $43.92 and $44.53 so far, and is at about $44.20–44.27.

### The bull case
- **Valuation has reset.** At about $44 the stock trades near 23 times fiscal 2027 EPS guidance, down from more than 100 times trailing earnings at the peak.
- **Usage is growing fast.** Customers' platform usage is up more than 20%. Log storage and analysis is growing more than 100% (about $250M a year). Infrastructure monitoring passed $500M a year, growing about 30%. Customers using AI use the platform at more than twice the rate of others.
- **The company is buying back stock.** In Q2 it bought back 5.2M shares at an average of $47.38, above today's price. About $1.3B of buyback authorization remains, roughly 10% of the company's value. Guidance doesn't include buybacks after Sept 30, so the company may be buying now; that is not confirmed.
- **Analysts kept their Buy ratings and trimmed targets only modestly:** DA Davidson cut to $60, BTIG to $63, Needham to $65 and BofA to $70. The consensus target is about $63.

### The bear case
- Delayed expansion deals and lower net retention may be the first sign of slowing growth. Renewals are heavily loaded into Q4 (about 65% of second-half renewals), so nothing will prove it either way until early February.
- Datadog's customer concentration has made investors doubt AI-driven monitoring spending across the sector.
- Profit guidance was cut, the CFO is leaving, and the broader software market was weak; the S&P 500 fell 3.9% over the same nine days.
- The convertible bond adds shares to the per-share math. Its buyers commonly hedge by shorting the stock, though I couldn't confirm how much of that is happening.

What the screen called "stretched down" is really a sideways base forming after the drop: the trading range is shrinking and selling volume is fading. The selling looks exhausted, but nothing in the story points to a reason for a rebound within days.

## Atlassian (TEAM): the story going into Monday, Nov 16, 2026

**In short:** TEAM roughly doubled after its August report. Its price peaked near $228 on Oct 23. It then lost about 35% in three weeks in two steps. First, a broad software and AI selloff took it from $228 to about $183 before earnings. Then on Nov 6 it gapped down about 16% when the company guided to slower growth despite beating the quarter. Since then it has gone sideways between about $145 and $155 for seven sessions. The low was $144.99, set intraday on Nov 10. Today it is pressing the bottom of that range in a weak tape. Nothing new has hit the company since the analyst price-target cuts.

### 1. How it got here
- **Before:** The stock fell from about $203 in mid-2025 to a low of about $56–68 by March 2026. That came in the "SaaSpocalypse": fear that AI agents will replace per-seat software licenses. On Apr 9 it fell 8.1% when Anthropic launched its Managed Agents product.
- **The rally:** On Aug 6 Atlassian reported fiscal Q4 2026 and raised guidance, with cloud growth reaccelerating to 31%. The stock jumped about 35% the next day, from $110 to $149, and Bank of America upgraded it to Buy. It kept climbing to a $229.96 intraday high on Oct 22 and a $227.61 close on Oct 23.
- **The pre-earnings slide (Oct 28 to Nov 5):** The stock fell from $220 to $183 with the whole sector. ServiceNow dropped about 27% on a weak contracted-revenue outlook, IGV (the iShares software ETF) fell, and a broad AI selloff hit around Nov 4–5.

### 2. The quarter (fiscal Q1 2027, reported after the close on Nov 5)
- **The beat:**
  - Revenue was $1.772B, up 24%, against an expected $1.71B.
  - Cloud revenue was $1.302B, up 31%.
  - Adjusted EPS was $1.65 against about $1.39–1.43 expected.
  - RPO (contracted future revenue) was $4.75B, up 44%. Current RPO grew 28%.
  - Free cash flow was $463M, a 26% margin.
  - GAAP operating margin was 11%, the second straight quarter of GAAP profit.
  - Buybacks were $588M in the quarter, up from $253M a year ago.
  - Net revenue retention was "well over" 120%. Over 87% of enterprise cloud customers use Rovo, its AI assistant.
- **What sank it:**
  - Full-year guidance calls for subscription ARR growth to slow to about 18.5% by June 2027, from 22.5–23% now.
  - Full-year revenue growth is guided to about 13.75%. That is lower partly because Data Center revenue is guided to fall about 16%: customers pulled Data Center purchases into fiscal 2026, and the product is retired in March 2029.
  - Billings grew 22.1%, behind revenue growth, and missed the billings forecast.
  - The CFO called the guide "prudent," citing macro and fiscal uncertainty and the timing of customer migrations. He also said the quarter's beat does not fully carry through to the full year, because of revenue-timing rules on hybrid deals.
  - Management says growth should pick up again in fiscal 2028 and that the guide is conservative. The market isn't giving it credit for that yet.
- **The AI question:** One analyst asked whether AI coding tools reduce the need for Jira and Confluence. The CEO said no: more agent work means more coordination, and seats from competitive wins grew over 40%. Usage-based pricing enforcement starts in early December, but management assumes no meaningful revenue from it in fiscal 2027.

### 3. Since the gap (Nov 6 to today)

The Nov 6 gap-day high of $165 sold off all session and has not been revisited. Every bounce since has stalled around $154–156. Volume is fading from 7.5M toward about 3M, which reads as a base forming, not as fresh forced selling.

### 4. Analysts: targets cut, ratings kept
Most firms lowered targets after the report but kept positive ratings:

| Firm | Old target | New target | Rating |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wells Fargo | $270 | $200 | Overweight |
| Truist | $250 | $200 | Buy |
| Jefferies | $245 | $190 | not stated |
| Citi | $245 | $220 | Buy |

Piper Sandler raised its target from $175 to $190 and TD Cowen from $145 to $180 (Hold); both had been below the market before the run-up. The consensus target is about $209–217, rated "Moderate Buy," roughly 40% above the price. No downgrade to Sell turned up.

### 5. Founders: one selling slowly, one reportedly buying
- **Farquhar selling:** On about Nov 10, co-founder Scott Farquhar (about 20% holder) filed a plan to sell 3,393,500 shares, spread out until Dec 4, 2027. That is roughly 13,000 shares a day, against 2–4M shares of normal daily volume, so it matters as a headline, not as daily supply.
- **Cannon-Brookes buying:** The same report says CEO Mike Cannon-Brookes is buying about US$250M of stock, partly Farquhar's shares. I could not confirm how: it may be a private transfer rather than open-market buying. My search budget ran out before I could check this, so treat it as a single-source claim.
- **Short interest:** The latest figure I found is from May 2026: 13.4M shares, 1.9 days to cover. I found nothing current.

### 6. This week's market backdrop
- **This morning:** Nasdaq-100 futures were down about 0.9–1.5% before the open. Chipmakers fell more than 5% premarket, Nvidia fell about 4% premarket, and Oracle about 4%. Oil was volatile on tanker incidents in the Strait of Hormuz. This came after the indexes' best week since August (each up more than 2%).
- **Nvidia earnings Tuesday, Nov 17, after the close:** These are its first results since CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week, and the stock is down more than 30% in five weeks.
- **Anthropic IPO:** It prices Wednesday, Nov 18, and starts trading Thursday, Nov 19 on Nasdaq as ANT, at about $1.4T. This is the main narrative risk for TEAM: Anthropic launches have hit TEAM before, and the IPO puts "AI replaces software seats" back in the headlines.
- **Possible rotation into software:** A Globe and Mail piece from Nov 13 says software names hit by AI-displacement fears are starting to recover as money leaves AI hardware. It doesn't mention Atlassian, and TEAM hasn't joined that move so far.
- **Usage-based pricing:** Enforcement starts in early December, possibly inside a 10-session window. Management says it won't add revenue this year, but it could still generate headlines.

### 7. What this means for a 1–10 session trade
- **For a bounce:**
  - The stock is already 35% off its high and the business is strong: cloud up 31%, RPO up 44%, 26% FCF margin, buybacks of about $590M a quarter.
  - Analysts kept their ratings, and the consensus target is about 40% higher.
  - The post-gap range is basing on fading volume, and a founder is reportedly adding about $250M.
  - Any rotation from AI hardware into software would help.
- **Against:**
  - The thing that broke is the growth path, with ARR growth slowing to about 18.5%, so cheapness alone may not bring buyers back.
  - The $145 floor is being tested today in a risk-off open.
  - Nvidia on Tuesday and the Anthropic IPO on Thursday are two big narrative events, either of which can push the sector either way.
  - The founder sale stays in the headlines, and the stock is very volatile: 51 moves of more than 5% in the past year.
- **Levels to watch:**
  - **$144.99 (Nov 10 low):** A clean break below it opens a move toward the $135–140 area. That target is my inference; I didn't research it.
  - **$154–156:** Where every bounce since the gap has stopped.
  - **$165:** The high of the gap day.
  - **$183:** The pre-earnings close, which would fill the gap.

**Discrepancies and gaps:**
- Sources disagree on the gap size (12% to 17%) and on the consensus EPS ($1.39 vs $1.43).

Oil has fallen hard from its war-time peak, and the broad market is being pulled down by an AI and chip sell-off. Today's +1.6% in the ratio is about 60% transports rising and 40% SPY falling. - **IYT:** $84.49, +0.97% (prior close $83.68). Its 52-week range is $68.10–$90.06, so IYT is still about 6% under its high. The stretch is in the ratio, not in IYT's own price.
